\begin{document}
\title{When the Attacker Is Indistinguishable from the Weather:\\
Provable Bounds on Undetected GNSS-Spoofing Deviation for UAVs}
\author{\IEEEauthorblockN{Paper \#XXX}
\IEEEauthorblockA{Submitted for double-blind review}}
\maketitle

% =====================================================================
\begin{abstract}
A UAV cannot tell from its navigation inputs whether a growing position error comes from a
jammer, a drifting sensor or wind, so an attacker can disguise interference as a tolerated
disturbance. We bound the probability that a mission fails with no detector raising an alarm, for
every coupling of the benign disturbances. For any causal, adaptive, fully informed GNSS-offset
attacker, a linear programme proves the largest undetected deviation of a linear navigation loop,
with finite-sample confidence. The bound is finite only when a trusted fix re-anchors the
estimator, and shrinks from \nBoundTaFive\,m at 5\,s to \nBoundTaOne\,m at 1\,s. In
\nMissionsTotal{} simulated missions, optimised disguises evade four detectors, and CUSUM barely
tightens the bound: detectors must tolerate benign noise. In \nPxMissions{} PX4
software-in-the-loop missions, the stealth budget transferred (\nPxDadv\,m against
\nPxDadvRoPilot--\nPxDadvRoPooled\,m) but the full disguise matrix did not; re-anchoring every
second kept every undetected deviation within \nPxTaWorstDOneGate\,m, inside the proved bound.
\end{abstract}

% =====================================================================
\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}
% =====================================================================
An autonomous UAV can be attacked through its command-and-control link, peer
mesh, on-board bus and navigation sensors.
Each interface has its own defences, with network intrusion detection
systems (IDSs) for the links and the
bus~\cite{zeng2025uavids,kim2022uavcan,whelan2020novelty}, physical-invariant
and residual monitors for the estimator~\cite{choi2018,quinonez2020savior,dash2019},
and certified robustness for learned
components~\cite{cohen2019smoothing,lecuyer2019}. None of them is designed
to show whether, once some attacks get through, the mission can still be
provably completed. For a single
declared attacker the question has a known answer, restated in
\cref{sec:background}, in which a Lipschitz--Gr\"onwall tube converts the
bounded navigation error caused by a relay delay just below a detector's
threshold into a certified floor on the mission-completion rate (MCR). This
answer assumes that the attacker is the only source of perturbation.

\paragraph{Attacks disguised as benign disturbances.}
Real navigation errors have many benign causes. A GNSS receiver drifts with
the ionosphere and multipath, an accelerometer bias steps or random-walks, and
wind pushes the airframe. Every monitor must therefore tolerate these
disturbances, and that tolerance is the space in which an attacker can hide.
Control-invariant monitors must accommodate deviation due to friction or
wind~\cite{dash2019}, and an actuator attack lying in the range of the
fault-input matrix is indistinguishable from a fault~\cite{roy2023}. A
GPS-only attacker can cause arbitrarily large deviation against any detector
when the closed loop is incrementally exponentially
stable~\cite{khazraei2024}, and a recent spoofer exploited a PX4 vehicle's
wind compensation to deviate it undetected~\cite{kim2024predictable}. From the
navigation input alone, shaped interference, a sensor fault and an
environmental disturbance can thus be indistinguishable, and an attacker will
choose the disguise that the defender models least well. A certificate gated on
detector silence is then unsound against an attacker who dresses as the
weather. A useful guarantee must instead be source-agnostic, bounding the
mission outcome whatever mixture of attack, fault, outage and wind produced the
perturbation, under any coupling.

\paragraph{What becomes possible.}
Spoofing detectors give an alarm, but no statement about the mission while the
alarm stays silent. Stealthy-attack reachability~\cite{mo2016,urbina2016}
bounds the error an attacker can cause under one residual detector, not under a
stack of heterogeneous detectors with benign disturbances of unknown dependence,
and not as a probability of mission failure. Control-invariant
detection~\cite{choi2018,quinonez2020savior} measures what an attacker achieves
undetected, without a proof for an adaptive attacker who chooses the disguise.
Runtime assurance~\cite{sha2001} switches to a safe controller once a monitor
fires, and gives no guarantee while the monitor is fooled. We bound the
probability of undetected mission failure for a stack of detectors under every
coupling of the benign disturbances, prove the undetected deviation for an
explicit adaptive attacker class, and show that the re-anchoring interval,
rather than any threshold, is the design parameter with a proved consequence.

\paragraph{Approach and contributions.}
We therefore replace the detection gate with a unified perturbation budget and
test the resulting bound against attackers optimised to evade it.
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{A threat model of adversarial equivalence (\cref{sec:threat}).}
  We define $\varepsilon$-observational equivalence, bound any detector's
  advantage by the total-variation (TV) distance (\cref{lem:lecam}), and show
  that an equivalent attack can violate a detector-gated certificate
  (\cref{prop:gated}). Unlike earlier work on fault
  mimicry~\cite{roy2023,bai2017,hashemi2018}, we let the attacker optimise
  the disguise.
\item \textbf{A unified budget with mixed semantics (\cref{sec:budget}).}
  $\dtot=\dnet(\theta)\oplus\dadv(\theta)\oplus\dgnss\oplus\dfault\oplus\denv$
  combines deterministic, stochastic and probability-box (p-box) terms. We prove
  a dependence-sharp bound on the probability of undetected mission failure
  (\cref{thm:floor}) and show when the union
  bound~\cite{makarov1981,ruschendorf1982} is sharp and when it is loose
  (\cref{prop:union}).
\item \textbf{A proved stealth budget (\cref{sec:certbudget}).} For every causal,
  adaptive GNSS-offset attacker, a linear programme bounds the undetected
  deviation; the bound is finite only with trusted re-anchoring and falls from
  \nBoundTaFive{} to \nBoundTaOne\,m as the interval shrinks from 5 to 1\,s.
\item \textbf{An evasion study and a soundness test
  (\cref{sec:evasion,sec:eval}).} We cross-evaluate attackers optimised over
  five disguises against four detectors, and test the bound on held-out
  attackers with negative controls.
\item \textbf{A negative result and its repair (\cref{sec:scaled,sec:revised}).}
  Stronger optimisers and a test scaled to \nROneTests{} points found the
  pilot instantiation unsound, with \nROneViol{} Holm-significant violations
  traced to two unsecured conditions unrelated to disguise. A run-time saturation
  alarm and a finite-sample p-box repair both.
\item \textbf{A pre-registered PX4 transfer study (\cref{sec:px4}).} In
  \nPxMissions{} SITL missions with EKF2, the stealth budget transferred, the
  pre-registered transfer of the full disguise matrix did not, and we report both.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{Scope.}
The main evaluation uses a reduced-order lateral multirotor model with a
Kalman filter (KF), and the proved budget holds for that linear loop.
\Cref{sec:px4} repeats the key experiments in PX4 software-in-the-loop (SITL)
simulation with its EKF2 estimator under a pre-registered protocol. Throughout,
``certified'' means proved under the conditions stated with the result.

% =====================================================================
\section{Preliminaries and Problem Statement}
\label{sec:prelim}
% =====================================================================
\input{fig_framework}
\subsection{Navigation loop and mission completion}
Let $x(t)\in\R^n$ be the navigation state of the aircraft and
$\dot x=F(x,u)$ its closed-loop dynamics under feedback $u$ computed from the
estimated state $\hat x$. A mission $\omega$ of horizon $T$ follows a
nominal path $x^{\mathrm{nom}}$ inside a corridor of half-width (margin) $m$.
Writing $e(t)$ for the cross-track deviation of the true position from the
nominal path, the mission completes if and only if
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:complete}
\textstyle \sup_{t\in[0,T]}|e(t)|\le m .
\end{equation}
The mission-completion rate is
$\MCR=\Pr_{\omega\sim\mathcal M}[\eqref{eq:complete}]$ for a stated mission
distribution $\mathcal M$; it is a population quantity, not a statement about
any single flight. \Cref{app:notation} collects the notation.

\subsection{Background: A certificate for delayed navigation input}
\label{sec:background}
This subsection states the certificate for a single attack class on which the
network term of our budget rests, together with its constants. The constants
are computed in the released artifact~\cite{artifact}: the rate $\gamma$ from
the real GPS jamming and spoofing flights of the UAV Attack
Dataset~\cite{whelan2020dataset}, and the slack $s$ and the local Lipschitz
estimate $L$ in the artifact's relay and dynamics analyses.

\emph{Tube.} Suppose $F$ is $L$-Lipschitz on the operating region (condition
C1), and the filter re-anchors on an uncorrupted update at least once every
certification horizon $T_c$ (condition C2). If a perturbation leaves an error of
at most $\delta$ in the state at the start of a window, the error then obeys
$\|\dot e\|\le L\|e\|$ with $\|e(0)\|\le\delta$, and Gr\"onwall's
inequality~\cite{gronwall1919} bounds the deviation over the window by the tube
radius $\rho=\delta e^{LT_c}$.

\emph{Hidden delay.} A multi-hop forwarding detector flags any hop whose
forwarding delay exceeds a per-hop threshold $\theta$, and a message that misses
its contact window, with slack $s$, is flagged regardless of the threshold. An
attacker controlling $H$ relays on a route can therefore hide at most
$\min(\theta,s)$ of delay per hop, and at most
$\Delta(\theta)\le H\min(\theta,s)$ of staleness in total. In the released detector replay, no
undetected per-hop delay exceeded \nParentSlack\,s over \nParentHops{} relay hops, below the
5\,s contact-window slack, and we use this measured cap for $s$.

\emph{Delay-to-position rate.} While the estimator waits for a delayed message,
its position error grows at a rate $\gamma$, evaluated at the supremum over 674
post-onset samples of the flights above, $\gamma=\nParentGamma$\,m/s. The
network contribution to the deviation is therefore at most
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:dnet}
e^{LT_c}\,\dnet(\theta),\qquad \dnet(\theta)=\gamma\,H\min(\theta,s),
\end{equation}
with $L=\nParentL$ and $T_c=1$\,s. At the operating point used throughout
($\theta=0.25$\,s, $H=2$) this contributes \nNetTubeQuarter\,m.

\subsection{Perturbation sources and their semantics}
Five sources perturb the navigation loop. They differ in magnitude and in the
kind of statement that can be made about them.

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabularx}{\columnwidth}{@{}l>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Term} & \textbf{Origin} & \textbf{Semantics} \\
\midrule
$\dnet(\theta)$ & relay delay below $\theta$ & deterministic worst case \\
$\dadv(\theta)$ & disguised GNSS offset below the detector stack at $\theta$ & deterministic worst case (stealth budget) \\
$\dgnss$ & noise, Gauss--Markov drift, outages, jamming noise & stochastic, known marginal \\
$\dfault$ & inertial bias steps and drift, actuator loss of effectiveness & stochastic, known marginal \\
$\denv$ & turbulence within a declared intensity range & bounded-unknown (p-box) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

\noindent
A deterministic term is a number that holds for every admissible behaviour. A
stochastic term has a cumulative distribution function (CDF) that we estimate
on a calibration split. A bounded-unknown term has a distribution known only to
lie between a lower and an upper CDF, a probability box~\cite{ferson2003}. For
wind, the box is spanned by the Dryden turbulence model of
MIL-F-8785C~\cite{milf8785c} between light and moderate intensity. The sources
do not, however, come with a joint distribution. Nature couples gusts and
outages in ways that have not been measured, and an attacker who induces
jamming can choose when GNSS degradation coincides with gusts.

\subsection{Problem statement}
Given (i)~the marginal laws of the stochastic sources, (ii)~an envelope for the
bounded-unknown source, (iii)~a detector stack operating at false-positive
rate (FPR) budget $\alpha$ with thresholds $\theta$, and (iv)~an attacker free
to choose both the shape of its interference and its coupling to the benign
sources, we seek:
\begin{description}[leftmargin=1.6em,style=sameline]
\item[P1] an upper bound on the probability that a mission fails
  and its attack goes undetected, valid for every coupling of the benign
  sources and every attacker, i.e., a source-agnostic bound;
\item[P2] a characterisation of how much tightness each aggregation rule
  sacrifices and where the slack comes from;
\item[P3] a measurement substrate that keeps the evidence behind every coupling
  explicit, and an evasion study that measures which disguise defeats which
  detector.
\end{description}
\noindent These define six research questions. RQ1: can an attacker mimic a
fault, a GNSS drift or a gust well enough to evade a detector while still
producing a large deviation, and which disguise does each detector miss? RQ2:
does the source-agnostic floor bound the outcome of missions whose attack went
undetected? RQ3: how loose are the union bound and the dependence-sharp bound in
practice, and is the looseness due to dependence or to time? RQ4: is the floor
sound at every held-out operating point under Holm-corrected tests, and does the
test detect unsoundness when a condition is deliberately broken? RQ5: does the
answer to RQ4 survive stronger attackers and a larger test, and if not, which
condition fails? RQ6: how much does the floor change when the simulated GNSS
marginal is replaced by measured jamming data?

\Cref{fig:framework} summarises the methodology through which the paper answers
these questions.

% =====================================================================
\section{Threat Model: Adversarial Equivalence}
\label{sec:threat}
% =====================================================================
\subsection{Capabilities, knowledge and goal}
The attacker can (a) delay relayed messages on up to $H$ hops of the mesh, as in
\cref{sec:background}, and (b) add an offset $d(t)$ to the GNSS position the
navigation filter receives. Capability (b) is realised in practice by
signal-level spoofing~\cite{humphreys2008,tippenhauer2011,kerns2014}; in this
paper it is exercised only through simulator interfaces. The attacker cannot
corrupt the inertial measurement unit (IMU), and it cannot corrupt a trusted
re-anchoring fix, such as a visual landmark or an authenticated position
broadcast, that arrives at least once every $T_a$ seconds (condition C2$'$, which
generalises the re-anchoring condition C2 of \cref{sec:background} from the
network channel to the GNSS channel). We return to IMU injection~\cite{son2015,trippel2017} in
\cref{sec:discussion}.

Following Kerckhoffs's principle, the attacker knows the detector designs and
their thresholds. It also observes the local wind, which a co-located attacker
can measure. It does not know the realisation of the benign noise. Its goal is to
maximise the vehicle's cross-track deviation while raising no alarm at any time
during the mission. Being detected late counts as being detected.

\subsection{Observational equivalence}
Let $O_{0:T}$ denote everything the defender observes: GNSS fixes, IMU samples,
commanded accelerations and anchor fixes. Write $P_a$ for the law of $O_{0:T}$
under attack $a$ (with the benign sources present), and $P_d$ for its law under a
benign disturbance $d$ drawn from a class $\Dclass$, such as inertial-bias drift,
GNSS multipath drift, or turbulence of a given intensity.

\begin{definition}[$\varepsilon$-observational equivalence]
\label{def:equiv}
Attack $a$ is $\varepsilon$-equivalent to the class $\Dclass$ if
$\inf_{d\in\Dclass}\TV(P_a,P_d)\le\varepsilon$, where
$\TV(P,Q)=\sup_A|P(A)-Q(A)|$ over measurable events $A$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Detection advantage; Le Cam]
\label{lem:lecam}
For every detector $\psi:O_{0:T}\to\{0,1\}$ and every $d\in\Dclass$,
$\Pr_a[\psi=1]\le\Pr_d[\psi=1]+\TV(P_a,P_d)\le\Pr_d[\psi=1]+\sqrt{\KL(P_a\|P_d)/2}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The event $\{\psi=1\}$ is measurable, so $|P_a(\psi=1)-P_d(\psi=1)|\le\TV(P_a,P_d)$
by definition. The second inequality is Pinsker's~\cite{tsybakov2009}.
\end{proof}

\noindent
\Cref{lem:lecam} unifies three earlier notions. The ``hidden'' attacks of Hashemi
et al.\ raise alarms at the false-alarm rate~\cite{hashemi2018}; the
$\varepsilon$-stealthy attacks of Bai et al.\ bound the Kullback--Leibler (KL)
divergence~\cite{bai2017}; and the fault-mimicking attacks of Roy and Dey are the
noiseless case $\varepsilon=0$ in which $\Dclass$ is a fault class~\cite{roy2023}.
A detector with false-alarm rate $\alpha$ on $\Dclass$ thus catches an
$\varepsilon$-equivalent attack with probability at most $\alpha+\varepsilon$,
whatever its design.

\begin{definition}[Disguise-optimal attacker]
\label{def:disguise}
For a detector stack $\Psi_\theta=\{\psi_{D,\theta_D}\}_D$ and disguise families
$\{\Dclass_k\}$, each parameterised by $\phi\in\Phi_k$, the attacker solves
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:attacker}
\delta^\star_k(\theta)=\sup_{\phi\in\Phi_k}\ \E\big[\,\Delta_\phi\cdot
\mathbb 1\{\psi_{D,\theta_D}(O^\phi)=0\ \forall D\}\big],
\end{equation}
where $\Delta_\phi=\sup_t|e(t)|$ is the induced deviation. It then selects
$k^\star(\theta)=\arg\max_k\delta^\star_k(\theta)$, so that $k^\star$ is the
disguise class the stack tolerates most.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Detector-gated certificates and equivalence]
\label{prop:gated}
Let $\psi$ have false-alarm probability at most $\alpha$ under every
$d\in\Dclass$, and let $f_\Dclass$ be a floor valid under $\Dclass$. Let $a$ be
$\varepsilon$-equivalent to $\Dclass$ with $\alpha+\varepsilon<1$, and let
$q_a=\Pr_a[\text{fail}\mid\psi=0]$. Then
\[
\MCR_a\;\le\;1-q_a\,(1-\alpha-\varepsilon).
\]
Hence $f_\Dclass$ is violated by $a$ whenever
$q_a(1-\alpha-\varepsilon)>1-f_\Dclass$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
By \cref{lem:lecam}, $\Pr_a[\psi=0]\ge\Pr_d[\psi=0]-\varepsilon\ge1-\alpha-\varepsilon$.
Then $1-\MCR_a\ge\Pr_a[\text{fail}\wedge\psi=0]=q_a\Pr_a[\psi=0]$.
\end{proof}

\noindent
A floor that is to remain valid against every such attack must therefore bound
the deviation the attack itself causes on undetected missions, because
detector silence is not evidence of a benign disturbance. The
proposition formalises the statement that ``the decisive attack is the one
that looks benign''. Without condition C2$'$, Khazraei et al.\ show that a
GPS-only attacker can make the undetected deviation grow without bound in an
incrementally exponentially stable closed loop~\cite{khazraei2024}, so $q_a$
approaches one for any fixed corridor. With C2$'$, the deviation an
undetected attacker can accumulate is limited by the anchor interval. The stealth budget
$\dadv(\theta)$ of \cref{sec:budget} is our estimate of that limit.

% =====================================================================
\section{The Unified Budget and the Source-Agnostic Floor}
\label{sec:budget}
% =====================================================================
\subsection{From sources to an additive budget}
For each benign source $i\in\{\mathrm{gnss},\mathrm{fault},\mathrm{env}\}$, let
$e_i(t)$ be the deviation the closed loop would exhibit under source $i$ alone,
and define its \emph{sup-deviation} $X_i=\sup_t|e_i(t)|$. Let $e_{\mathrm{adv}}$
be the deviation under the attack alone.

\begin{lemma}[Sub-additivity for additive inputs]
\label{lem:subadd}
Fix the time-varying parameters of a mission (GNSS outage schedule, actuator
effectiveness, anchor schedule). If the closed loop is then linear in its
additive inputs (wind force, sensor noise and bias, attack offset), the
deviation decomposes as $e=e_{\mathrm{ben}}+e_{\mathrm{adv}}$, and
$\sup_t|e(t)|\le\sup_t|e_{\mathrm{ben}}(t)|+\sup_t|e_{\mathrm{adv}}(t)|$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Superposition for a linear time-varying system, then the triangle inequality.
\end{proof}

\noindent
Two remarks limit the scope of the lemma. First, actuator saturation is not linear,
so the lemma holds only inside the region where (C1) holds, and (C1) excludes
saturation from that region for this reason.
Second, outages and loss of effectiveness are \emph{parametric} sources: they
change the system rather than add an input. The further decomposition of
$e_{\mathrm{ben}}$ into per-source suprema,
$\sup_t|e_{\mathrm{ben}}|\le\sum_iX_i$, is therefore an assumption, which we
state as condition (C5) and test mission by mission in \cref{sec:eval}.

\subsection{Dependence-sharp aggregation}
Because the $X_i$ share no known joint law, we bound the tail of their sum over
all couplings consistent with the marginals. For non-negative $X_1,\dots,X_d$
with survival functions $S_i(t)=\Pr[X_i>t]$, define the worst-case and standard bounds
\begin{align}
\pbar(s)&=\sup_{C}\Pr_C\Big[\textstyle\sum_{i}X_i>s\Big],\\
p_U(s)&=\min\Big\{1,\ \inf_{s_1+\dots+s_d=s}\textstyle\sum_iS_i(s_i)\Big\},
\end{align}
where the supremum runs over all copulas $C$.

\begin{proposition}[Tightness of the union bound]
\label{prop:union}
(a)~$\pbar(s)\le p_U(s)$ for all $s$.
(b)~For $d=2$, $\pbar=p_U$ at every continuity point: the union bound is
sharp~\cite{makarov1981,ruschendorf1982,frank1987}.
(c)~For $d\ge3$ the inequality can be strict.
(d)~Against a known benign coupling $C_0$, the ratio
$p_U(s)/\Pr_{C_0}[\sum X_i>s]$ never exceeds $d$ under comonotonicity (take
$s_i=F_i^{-1}(u)$) and equals $d$ for identically distributed comonotone sources
whenever the equal split is optimal. Under independence it is unbounded: for two independent
$\mathrm{Exp}(1)$ sources, $p_U(s)\approx2e^{-s/2}$ while the truth is
$(1+s)e^{-s}$.
(e)~A deterministic term $X_j\equiv c$ has a single coupling with any other
variable, so it shifts $s$ by $c$ and contributes no dependence gap.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
(a) For any split, $\{\sum X_i>s\}\subseteq\bigcup_i\{X_i>s_i\}$. (b) is
Makarov's theorem~\cite{makarov1981}, proved independently by
R\"uschendorf~\cite{ruschendorf1982}; Frank et al.\ give the
attaining coupling~\cite{frank1987}. (c) Embrechts et al.\ give examples of
strict inequality~\cite{embrechts2013var}. (d) is direct
computation; for independent exponentials, $p_U$ is attained at the equal split
and the ratio $2e^{s/2}/(1+s)$ diverges (\cref{app:proofs}). (e) The Fr\'echet
class of a Dirac marginal is a singleton.
\end{proof}

\noindent
For $d\ge3$, the Rearrangement Algorithm (RA) approximates $\pbar$ with
excellent empirical accuracy but without a general convergence
proof~\cite{puccetti2012,embrechts2013var}.

\paragraph{Control of the coupling.}
The adversarial offset enters as a deterministic term, so by (e) it has no
coupling to choose. The dependence-sharp bound is needed for two other
reasons. First, nature's coupling of gusts, outages and faults has never been
measured. Second, an attacker who controls a stochastic source, for
example by jamming to induce the outages and noise of $\dgnss$, chooses when
that source fires relative to the others, and hence its coupling, provided the
induced episodes leave the marginal of $X_{\mathrm{gnss}}$ within its
calibration (C3). A common intuition holds that a joint treatment recovers the
union bound's slack precisely when the sources are comonotone.
\Cref{prop:union} shows otherwise.
When the coupling is unknown or adversarial, the union bound is already the
right quantity for two sources and nearly right for three, and slack exists
only relative to a coupling that is known to be benign.

\subsection{The floor}
\begin{theorem}[Source-agnostic, dependence-sharp bound]
\label{thm:floor}
Assume (C1)~a Lipschitz, unsaturated closed loop; (C2$'$)~a trusted re-anchoring
fix at least every $T_a$ seconds, including at the end of the mission; (C3)~transfer
of the calibrated interface quantities ($\gamma$, the marginals of $X_i$, and
the stealth budget $\dadv$) to the deployment; (C4)~an environmental marginal in
the declared envelope, with CDFs
$\underline F_{\mathrm{env}}\le F_{\mathrm{env}}\le\overline F_{\mathrm{env}}$;
(C5)~sub-additivity across benign sources; and (C6)~additivity of the network
contribution, bounded by $e^{LT_c}\dnet(\theta)$, to the others. Let $U$ be the event that the stack
$\Psi_\theta$ raises no alarm. Then, for every coupling of the benign sources and
every attack,
\begin{align}
\Pr[\text{fail}\wedge U]\ &\le\ \pbar\big(s_m\big),\qquad
s_m=m-e^{LT_c}\dnet(\theta)-\dadv(\theta),\label{eq:floor}
\end{align}
with $\pbar$ evaluated at the stochastically largest environmental marginal,
whose CDF is $\underline F_{\mathrm{env}}$. Consequently
$\Pr[\text{complete}\mid U]\ge1-\pbar(s_m)/\Pr[U]$, and in the population of
all missions $\Pr[\text{fail}\wedge U]\le1-f(m)$ with $f(m)=1-\pbar(s_m)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
On $U$, (C3) gives $\sup_t|e_{\mathrm{adv}}|\le\dadv$, and \eqref{eq:dnet} bounds
the network contribution by $e^{LT_c}\dnet(\theta)$, which adds to the others
by (C6) (\cref{lem:subadd} does not cover the network term). By \cref{lem:subadd} and
(C5), failure on $U$ implies $\sum_iX_i>s_m$. Hence
$\Pr[\text{fail}\wedge U]\le\Pr[\sum_iX_i>s_m]\le\pbar(s_m)$, which needs no
conditioning on $U$. The tail of a sum is non-decreasing under first-order
stochastic dominance of any summand, for every coupling and hence for the
supremum, so the stochastically largest member of the p-box is the worst
(\cref{app:proofs}). The conditional form follows by dividing by $\Pr[U]$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The theorem is conditional in the same sense as the delay certificate of
\cref{sec:background}: its first and last links are proved, and its
interface quantities are measured. We therefore test (C3)--(C5) empirically
in \cref{sec:eval} instead of asserting them. For the adversarial input of (C3),
the proved budget of \cref{sec:certbudget} can replace the measured one; it
holds for every attacker in its class on the linear loop. Bounding the joint event
$\{\text{fail}\wedge U\}$, rather than the completion rate conditional on
silence, allows the bound to use unconditional benign marginals, since
conditioning on silence would select benign realisations and change their law.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Computing the floor}
The marginals are estimated on a calibration split (seed block 1xxx) from
\nCalMissions{} missions per source. $p_U$ is minimised over a grid of splits.
$\pbar$ is approximated by the RA with $N=1{,}000$ quantile levels, using both the
upper and the lower discretisation, keeping the larger value, and bisecting on
the confidence level~\cite{embrechts2013var,hofert2020}; \cref{app:ra} gives the
procedure. $p_U$ is a proven upper
bound on $\pbar$; the RA value, with the conservative discretisation, is a
numerical approximation of $\pbar$ that is not proven in general. We report
$\min(\mathrm{RA},p_U)$ as our estimate of $\pbar$, which also removes the RA's
$1/N$ resolution floor in the far tail, and we give $p_U$ alongside wherever a
bound must be strictly certified. For reference only, we
also report the tail under independence (Monte Carlo) and under comonotonicity
(quantile sum); neither is a certificate.

\subsection{A proved stealth budget for an explicit attacker class}
\label{sec:certbudget}
\Cref{thm:floor} takes $\dadv$ as an input. An empirical supremum over
optimised attackers is only a lower bound on it (\cref{sec:scaled}), so we
also prove an upper bound for a stated class of attackers.

\begin{definition}[Attacker class $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{GNSS}}$]
An attacker in $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{GNSS}}$ chooses one GNSS position offset $d_j$
per GNSS epoch, causally and adaptively, with full knowledge of the model,
the noise realisation and every threshold. It cannot alter the IMU, the actuators
or the trusted re-anchoring fix.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Uniform proved budget]
\label{prop:certbudget}
On the linear loop of \cref{sec:evasion}, on a mission with constant loss of
effectiveness and no GNSS outage, let
$\Psi$ contain D1, the anchor gate and the saturation alarm $D_{\mathrm{sat}}$.
Let each of the $m$ benign margins be the order statistic of $N$ calibration
missions that upper-bounds its $1-\epsilon/m$ quantile with confidence
$1-\delta/m$. Then, with confidence at least $1-\delta$ over the calibration sample
and probability at least $1-\epsilon$ over the benign inputs, every attack in $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{GNSS}}$ that leaves $\Psi$ silent has
$\sup_t|e_{\mathrm{adv}}(t)|\le\delta_{\mathrm{cert}}(T_a)$, the value of the
linear programme of \cref{sec:revised}.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
By superposition (\cref{lem:subadd}, exact on the event $U$ because
$D_{\mathrm{sat}}$ is silent), the attack-only deviation and the attack-only parts
of the detector statistics are linear in $d$. Silence of each detector in $\Psi$, together with
the benign margins, implies a convex (here polyhedral) constraint on $d$. The
bound holds for every $d$ in the feasible set, which contains every sequence an
adaptive policy can produce on that realisation. The order statistic
$X_{(k)}$ falls below the $q$-quantile only if at least $k$ of the $N$ samples do,
with probability $P(\mathrm{Bin}(N,q)\ge k)\le\delta/m$ for any continuous
distribution; union bounds over the $m$ margins give the confidence and the
probability.
\end{proof}

\noindent
\emph{Finite only with trusted re-anchoring.} At $T_a=5$\,s and 1\% FPR the
programme is \nREightGateOnly{} with the anchor gate alone, an attacker that
carries the estimate along with the vehicle passes every fix,
\nREightDOneFiveOnePct\,m with D1 added, and \nREightSatFive\,m with
$D_{\mathrm{sat}}$. (These values use large-sample margins.) Without the trusted fix it is unbounded with D1 and
\nREightNoAnchorSat\,m with $D_{\mathrm{sat}}$, limited only by the mission
length. A useful worst case for $\mathcal A_{\mathrm{GNSS}}$ thus needs both the
fix and the saturation alarm.

\emph{The benign envelope is the attacker's budget.} D3 is convex after all:
its CUSUM stays below $\theta_3$ if and only if every window sum of squared
residuals stays below $\theta_3+(1+\kappa)|W|$, which with the triangle
inequality gives second-order-cone constraints. With the margins split over
these constraints as well, adding them moves the bound only from
\nDThreeWithout{} to \nDThreeWith\,m (at $t=\nDThreeEvalT$\,s), because $\theta_3\approx\nDThreeTheta$ must admit
benign jamming noise and outages. D2 and D4 alarm on runs of exceedances, which
need mixed-integer constraints; omitting them keeps the bound valid.

\emph{A design rule with a proof.} \Cref{tab:boundta} gives the proved budget
against the re-anchoring interval. It falls almost linearly, so re-anchoring
every second certifies a 20\,m corridor against every attacker in
$\mathcal A_{\mathrm{GNSS}}$, and every 0.5\,s a 10\,m corridor, before the network
tube and the benign floor of \cref{thm:floor} are subtracted. The scope is the
linear loop. The margins are distribution-free (the \nConfRank th largest of
\nConfN{} calibration values, $\delta=\nConfDelta$) and raise the bound by at most
\nConfIncMax{} over large-sample quantiles. \Cref{sec:px4} checks the bound against PX4.

\section{Cross-Layer Experimental Substrate}
\label{sec:benchmark}
% =====================================================================
The evaluation runs on a cross-layer event schema released in the
artifact~\cite{artifact}, whose records join a network or environmental window
to the navigation window it induces. For this paper we add a
\code{perturbation\_source} field (\code{net}, \code{gnss}, \code{fault},
\code{env}, \code{adv}), and every pairing carries a provenance flag:
\code{measured\_same\_platform}, \code{physics\_model} or
\code{synthetic\_alignment}. Adapters ingest the HCRL UAVCAN
corpus~\cite{kim2022uavcan}, UAVIDS-2025~\cite{zeng2025uavids}, a replay of the
DATAMUt detector~\cite{soltani2026datamut}, the UAV Attack
Dataset~\cite{whelan2020dataset,whelan2020novelty} and
UAV-EW-Bench~\cite{uavewbench2026}; an adapter for
UAV-CAS~\cite{mishra2026uavcas} is included, but its release could not be
retrieved for this study. Together they give \nEventsTotal{} events
(\nEventsReal{} from real hardware), and the number of released
\code{measured\_same\_platform} pairings is zero. Fault and environment
sources follow the RflyMAD~\cite{le2025rflymad} and ALFA~\cite{keipour2021alfa}
taxonomies and the Dryden model~\cite{milf8785c}. The substrate supplies the
constants of the network term ($\gamma$, $s$, $L$; \cref{sec:background}); the
evasion study runs in simulation and is flagged \code{synthetic\_alignment}.
Third-party corpora are fetched from their origin under their own licences.

% =====================================================================
\section{Evasion Study Design}
\label{sec:evasion}
% =====================================================================
\subsection{Closed loop and perturbation models}
The pilot models the lateral (cross-track) channel of a small multirotor
cruising at $V=8$\,m/s through a 60\,s mission segment. The airframe is a
drag-damped double integrator, $\ddot p=u+c_d(w-\dot p)$ with $c_d=0.35$\,s$^{-1}$.
It is driven by a proportional--derivative (PD) controller acting on the KF
estimate and saturated at 4\,m/s$^2$. The KF has states (position, velocity,
accelerometer bias), propagates with the 20\,Hz accelerometer, and corrects
with 10\,Hz GNSS fixes and the anchor fix every $T_a=5$\,s.
\Cref{app:constants} lists the simulator constants.

\emph{Environment.} The lateral wind $w$ follows the Dryden spectrum of
MIL-F-8785C at 100\,ft altitude. With $W_{20}$ the wind speed at 20\,ft, it has
$\sigma_v=0.1W_{20}/(0.177+0.000823h)^{0.4}$ and scale length
$L_v=h/(0.177+0.000823h)^{1.2}$. The declared envelope is
$W_{20}\in[15,30]$\,kt (light to moderate); severe turbulence (45--60\,kt) lies
outside it and serves as a negative control. Because the accelerometer measures
the aerodynamic force, wind is consistent between the IMU and GNSS, as it is on
a real airframe to first order.

\emph{Faults.} Faults are drawn independently per mission: an accelerometer bias
step (probability 0.3, $\sigma=0.1$\,m/s$^2$); bias drift (0.2, with the random
walk inflated tenfold); and actuator loss of effectiveness (LoE) of 10--30\%
(0.2).

\emph{GNSS.} Noise has a white component ($\sigma=0.5$\,m) and a first-order
Gauss--Markov drift ($\sigma=0.8$\,m, $\tau=60$\,s). Outages are
exponential with mean 5\,s (probability 0.3), and jamming-noise episodes
triple $\sigma$ for 10\,s (probability 0.2).

\subsection{Detectors}
All four detectors observe only $O_{0:T}$. Each reduces a mission to one
statistic $S_D$ and alarms when $S_D>\theta_D$:
\begin{description}[leftmargin=1em,style=nextline]
\item[D1, signature monitor.] $S_1=\max_k|z_k-z_{k-1}|$, the largest jump between
  consecutive fixes. It stands in for rule-based IDSs tuned to malicious
  signatures such as jumps and discontinuities.
\item[D2, $\chi^2$ innovation gate.] This is loosely modelled on innovation
  gating in PX4-class filters: it alarms when the normalised innovation squared
  (NIS) $\nu_k^2/S_k$ exceeds $\theta_2$ on three consecutive fixes. (PX4's EKF2
  rejects individual measurements rather than alarming.)
\item[D3, SAVIOR-style CUSUM.] A model-based observer driven by the commanded
  acceleration with a no-wind model accumulates a cumulative-sum (CUSUM)
  statistic $g_k=\max(0,g_{k-1}+r_k^2-(1+\kappa))$ on its GNSS
  residual~\cite{quinonez2020savior}.
\item[D4, IMU--GNSS invariant.] A quadratic is fitted over 4\,s to the residual
  between the GNSS position and the doubly integrated accelerometer; the
  detector alarms when the curvature, an acceleration discrepancy, exceeds
  $\theta_4$ on five consecutive fixes. It is the cross-sensor analogue of the
  control invariants of Choi et al.~\cite{choi2018}.
\end{description}
Whenever C2$'$ holds, an anchor gate on the anchor fix's NIS (calibrated FPR
1\%) is part of every stack. Thresholds are set on \nCalMissions{} benign
missions so that each detector has the stated per-mission FPR; the combined
stack \textsc{All} splits the budget equally among its four members.

\subsection{Disguise families and the attacker}
The offset $d(t)$, applied from an onset time $t_0$, belongs to one of five
families:
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{step}: $d=A$ (the naive spoofer);
\item \emph{ramp}: $d=\min\{r(t-t_0),A\}$ (the ``boiling frog'');
\item \emph{fault mimic}: $\ddot d=\beta_0+\beta(t)$, with $\beta$ a random walk,
  capped at $|d|\le A$. It imitates accelerometer-bias drift, which the filter's
  bias state absorbs;
\item \emph{GNSS mimic}: $d=A|g(t)|+c(t-t_0)$, with $g$ a unit Gauss--Markov
  process of attacker-chosen correlation time, imitating multipath or
  ionospheric drift;
\item \emph{weather mimic}: $d=A\,w(t-\ell)/\sigma_{\mathrm{mod}}+b\min\{(t-t_0)/10,1\}$,
  where $\sigma_{\mathrm{mod}}$ is the moderate-turbulence $\sigma_v$. The offset
  follows the true gust with a lag $\ell$.
\end{itemize}
The attacker solves~\eqref{eq:attacker} with the cross-entropy method
(CEM)~\cite{rubinstein2004cem}: 12 candidates per generation, 4 elites,
\nCemGens{} generations and \nCemK{} missions per candidate. Each
(stack $\times$ family $\times$ operating point) combination gets its own
optimiser seed in block 2xxx; stronger optimisers (CMA-ES~\cite{hansen2016cma},
Bayesian optimisation) are the subject of the scaled attacker study
(\cref{sec:scaled}). Because a local optimiser can fail
to find an evading parameterisation that exists, we do not read detector
strength off the optimiser's own target. Instead, we \emph{cross-evaluate} every
optimised attacker against every stack.

\subsection{Metrics and statistical protocol}
For each optimised attacker, evaluated on fresh missions (block 4xxx), we report:
\begin{itemize}
\item the \emph{evasion rate} (no alarm at any point in the mission);
\item the attack's own contribution $\sup_t|e_{\mathrm{adv}}|$ on evading
  missions, computed on the same realisation with the additive benign inputs set
  to zero but the parametric ones (outages, LoE) kept, as in \cref{lem:subadd};
\item the Kolmogorov--Smirnov (KS) distance between each detector's statistic
  under attack and under benign conditions, a finite-sample estimate of the TV
  distance of \cref{lem:lecam} restricted to threshold tests.
\end{itemize}
In the cross-evaluated disguise matrix, a cell's contribution is the maximum
over attackers that evade in at least 5\% (and at least 10) of missions; we
report the unfiltered maxima separately. The stealth budget $\dadv(\theta)$ is
the supremum of the attack-only deviation over all evading missions, with
no such filter. It is pooled over all \nPooledAttackers{} optimised
attackers on calibration missions (block 1xxx). Every attacker uses the same
missions at every operating point, and an attack that is stealthy against
stricter thresholds is also stealthy against looser ones, so the pooled
supremum is monotone in the operating point by construction.

For soundness, we re-optimise an independent attacker with fresh seeds (block
3xxx) for every family and FPR, against the full stack. We evaluate it on $n=\nEvalMissions$
fresh missions per operating point, crossing family, FPR, wind (light, moderate,
envelope), margin $m$ and $\theta_{\mathrm{net}}$. The theorem's event is
$\{\text{fail}\wedge U\}$, so we count its occurrences $k$ and compute the
one-sided binomial $p$-value of $H_0{:}\ \Pr[\text{fail}\wedge U]\le\pbar(s_m)$.
The $p$-values are adjusted across all operating points by Holm's
procedure~\cite{holm1979}, and a violation is a Holm-adjusted $p<0.05$. We
also report the MCR conditional on $U$, with Clopper--Pearson
intervals~\cite{clopper1934}.
